items.where: No paper states this quantitative constant. Closest: Bertanha-Moreira (2020) Thm 3 / eq (2.6)-(2.8); Dufour (1997) Thm 3.x; Gleser-Hwang (1987); Kline-Masten arXiv:2504.14127 Sec 7.1 (identification-only remark that non-sampled values can be anything).
items.reason: The lemma is correct and the constant is UNCONDITIONAL; the two earlier reviewers are wrong. Proof check: for any fixed M let A={theta(z)+M/G in C(D)} (A does not depend on j). Perturbing z_j by M gives z' with theta(z')=theta+M/G and identical data on {j not in S}, so P_z(j not in S, A)=P_z'(j not in S, theta' in C(D')) >= (1-alpha)-n/G. Sum over j: sum_j 1{j not in S}=G-n in every sample, so sum_j P(j not in S, A)=(G-n)P(A) (A is the same event for every j; no conditioning on j happens). Hence P(A)>=(1-alpha-n/G)/(1-n/G). Caveat: the perturbed population z' must be an admissible population, so the lemma needs coverage over ALL z in R^G (kappa0=1 / no restriction); under coverage only on K(kappa0) it cannot be used because a spike of size M leaves K. The technique is the classical 'indistinguishable on an event' argument; I label it not_found because I found no printed statement with this constant, but it is an elementary consequence of the Gleser-Hwang/Dufour/BM principle and should not be sold as a result.

items.reason: True; short proof by Cauchy-Schwarz: with B constant of size G-k and deviation delta_B, complement deviations sum to -(G-k)delta_B, so sum d^2 >= (G-k)^2 delta_B^2/k; the largest complement share >= S2/(k(S2+(G-k)delta_B^2)) is increasing in S2, giving >= (1-k/G)/k with equality iff complement deviations are equal. The B-cluster share is <= k/(G(G-k)) <= kappa2(k) iff k<=G/2, which is the condition needed for equality to be the overall max-share. The inequality kappa>=kappa2(k) holds for every k in 1..G-1 (numerically checked by minimisation for G=6,8,9, all k: tight for k<=G/2, slack above); the 'equality iff' needs k<=G/2 as you bracketed.

items.reason: I verified the proof line by line and it is sound (for S in B1 take a=0,b=eps; for S in B2 take a=1,b=eps; coverage at z_eps in K (kappa(z_eps)->kappa2(k)<kappa0) forces C(S,z_S,f) to contain points near lambda*Fbar+k/(G eps) resp. lambda*Fbar-(G-k)/(G eps); limsup of events has probability >= pi(k)-alpha). Hendriks et al. contain only the one-line observation that for the symmetric +-1 Bernoulli law P(T_n=inf)=P(X1=...=Xn)=2^(1-n)>alpha when n<1-log(alpha)/log 2, so no finite t works for the t-interval; no theorem, no other procedures, no equivariance class, no finite population. It is therefore a special case of Theorem 1's G->infinity, k=G/2 boundary restricted to t-intervals, not the other way round. Lanke/Paul-Kuchibhotla give the median/shift-invariant version (threshold log2(1/alpha) proved, log2(2/alpha) conjectured). Caveat for your text: the technique (BM Thm 3) is classical; the novelty is the (E)-equivariant, finite-population, probability-graded form. Also: without (E) the same argument gives unboundedness only for z with e constant on B1 (or B2); (E) is what extends it to every z.

Structural analogue: Potscher-Preinerstorfer arXiv:2412.17470 Thm 2.2 (existence of a finite size-controlling critical value iff no hat-diagonal-1 row enters the restriction) and their 2018 J. Econometrics / 2025 Econometric Theory framework (invariance under the same location-scale group as (E), concentration/limit argument).
items.reason: Proof re-checked and correct: T is invariant under the affine maps, so reduce to compact {ebar=0, sum e^2=1, kappa<=kappa0} (closed and excludes constants); |T|>c forces s_S->0 with |ebar_S| bounded, so limit point e* is constant on the N=floor(alpha*C(G,n))+1 pigeonholed samples, contradicting #const<=beta*C<=floor(alpha*C). PP's setting differs: Gaussian heteroskedastic regression, tests of one linear restriction, degeneracy is a probability-0/1 event so the threshold is a yes/no condition (no leverage-1 point), whereas here degeneracy has a positive sampling probability and the condition is graded (beta<=alpha).

Lower bound is the two-point population (Lemma 1). Upper bound: a level-set partition whose largest block has size m>=G/2 has kappa>=kappa2(G-m) (Lemma 1) and count <= C(m,n)+C(G-m,n)=pi(G-m)C(G,n); if all blocks have size < G/2, convexity (majorisation) gives count <= floor(G/m)C(m,n)+C(G mod m,n) with m the largest block. I verified the sandwich by exhaustive enumeration of all integer partitions of G=8,10,12 with numerically minimised kappa per partition (90 (G,n,kappa0) cases, n=2,3,4): the sandwich held in all 90 and beta equalled the lower bound max pi(k) in all 90 (the R term never bound in this range).

Correct and elementary: for fixed S the number of size-k sets B2 with S in B2 is C(G-n,k-n) and with S in B2^c is C(G-n,k); dividing by C(G,k) gives C(k,n)/C(G,n) and C(G-k,n)/C(G,n), so the average over B2 of P_p(S in B1 or B2) equals pi(k) for EVERY design (identity checked numerically for G up to 29, n=2..5). Hence max over B2 >= pi(k), with equality for SRSWOR, i.e. SRSWOR is minimax-optimal for this barrier. Theorem 1's proof carries over verbatim with P_p.

what_the_finite_population_form_adds: (1) Boundary vs iid: Hendriks et al. give only the point 2^(1-n)>alpha for t-intervals and a single law. Here: the same number arises as the limit pi(G/2)->2^(1-n) for ALL (E)-equivariant procedures (not just t-intervals), but the finite-population structure adds a graded frontier: impossibility for every kappa0>kappa2(k*) where k*=max{k<=G/2: pi(k)>alpha}, possibility for kappa0<kappa2(k*) when R<=alpha, with the exact tie kappa0=kappa2(k*) left to Thm 2 failing. (2) Vs Potscher-Preinerstorfer: their threshold is a yes/no leverage condition because Gaussian degeneracy has probability 0 or 1; the SRSWOR sampling law gives degeneracy probability pi(k) in (0,1), so the condition becomes a quantitative comparison pi(k) vs alpha, tied to a max-share class (the max-share kappa is Hajek's Lindeberg condition m_N/v_N, which governs asymptotic normality; here it governs finite-sample boundedness). (3) Corrections to the CONSEQUENCE block (computed): G=24,n=8: k*=5 (pi(5)=0.1028>0.10), so impossibility for kappa0>kappa2(5)=0.1583 and possibility for every kappa0<0.1583 (R=0.00045); kappa2(6)=0.125 is only the largest jump point of beta, not the largest admissible kappa0 (sup is 0.1583, not attained). G=51,n=8: k*=11 (pi(11)=0.1208), threshold kappa2(11)=0.0713 (pi(12)=0.0966, kappa2(12)=0.0637 is the jump point). G=51,n=4: pi(k)>0.10 for all k<=25 (pi(25)=0.1104), threshold kappa2(25)=0.0204 which is also the minimum attainable kappa for odd G=51, so every nonempty class is impossible. (4) The asymptotic sentence is misleading: with n fixed and kappa0 fixed, G->infinity forces k about 1/kappa0 (constant) and pi(k)->1, so impossibility holds for EVERY n>=2 and every fixed kappa0<1 (e.g. kappa0=0.1,n=8: pi(10)=0.42 at G=100, 0.92 at G=1000, 0.992 at G=10000). The condition 2^(1-n)>alpha is the condition for impossibility at every nonempty class including kappa0 just above its minimum 1/G; when 2^(1-n)<=alpha, possibility requires kappa0*G below a constant c*(n,alpha) solving (c/(1+c))^n+(1/(1+c))^n=alpha (c*=3.0 for n=8, alpha=0.1; 4.7 for n=12; 8.2 for n=20), i.e. kappa0 of order 1/G, consistent with Hajek's CLT regime kappa<<min(n,G-n)/G. (5) Honest assessment: Lemma 0, Lemma 1, Prop 3, Cor 4 are elementary; Thm 1's mechanism is the classical Bahadur-Savage/Gleser-Hwang/Dufour/BM argument, so the contribution is the finite-population, (E)-equivariant, probability-graded statement plus the matching possibility theorem, not the impossibility idea itself.

closest_papers.citation: Hendriks, IJzerman-Boon, Klaassen (2006) Student's t-statistic under unimodal densities, Austrian J. Statist. 35(2&3):131-141
closest_papers.how_read: full text, all 11 pages (downloaded from ajs.or.at after network grant)
closest_papers.what_it_does: Edgeworth, tail and finite-sample analysis of t-intervals over symmetric unimodal laws; least favourable law is uniform for large nominal level.
closest_papers.overlap: Only a remark after eq. (7): symmetric +-1 Bernoulli has P(T_n=inf)=2^(1-n), so for n<1-log(alpha)/log2 no bounded t-interval exists. Matches the iid G->inf boundary of Thm 1 but for t-intervals only, as a remark without proof or generality.

closest_papers.citation: Potscher, Preinerstorfer, A necessary and sufficient condition for size controllability of heteroskedasticity robust test statistics, arXiv:2412.17470v5 (Econometric Theory FirstView 2026)
closest_papers.how_read: full text Sections 1-2, Remark 2.2, appendix lemmas A.1 ff; remainder keyword-scanned (no finite-population/sampling/unbounded content)
closest_papers.what_it_does: Gaussian heteroskedastic regression, single restriction: finite size-controlling critical value exists iff no hat-matrix-diagonal-1 row is involved (Thm 2.2), otherwise size 1 for every C; smallest critical value and lower bound C*.
closest_papers.overlap: Same invariance group as (E) and a concentration/limit-point mechanism, so Thm 1/2 are the sampling-design analogue; no finite population, no graded probability threshold, no confidence-set unboundedness.

closest_papers.citation: Paul, Kuchibhotla, Inference for median and a generalization of HulC, arXiv:2403.06357 (Remark 1; citing Lanke 1974, Scand. J. Statist.)
closest_papers.how_read: Remark 1 and intro read in text; Lanke 1974 itself NOT retrieved
closest_papers.what_it_does: Shift-invariant bounded CIs for a median when n>=log2(2/alpha); states Lanke's impossibility is proved only for n<log2(1/alpha) and conjectures none exists below log2(2/alpha).
closest_papers.overlap: Iid analogue of the 2^(1-n) boundary for shift-invariant intervals; their open conjecture is the median analogue of what Thm 1 proves for (E)-equivariant mean procedures in the two-point limit.

closest_papers.citation: Bertanha, Moreira (2020) Impossible inference in econometrics, J. Econometrics 218:247-270
closest_papers.what_it_does: If models with unbounded parameter range share a common limit law P*, valid sets must have P*[D=inf]>=1-alpha and be unbounded with positive probability nearby.
closest_papers.overlap: General principle behind Lemma 0 and Thm 1 (also Gleser-Hwang 1987, Dufour 1997). Needs weak-convergence/continuity conditions; no finite population or graded constant.

closest_papers.citation: Dutz, Zhang, Limitations of randomization tests in finite samples, arXiv:2512.07099v3
closest_papers.what_it_does: Characterises nulls that admit randomization tests; mean-zero null admits none (iid, finite or continuous support).
closest_papers.overlap: None on confidence-set boundedness or finite populations; cites Bahadur-Savage only.
